# Paper Plaine

> arXiv research papers explained in plain English, updated twice daily.

## What this site is

Paper Plaine surfaces fresh academic research from Cornell University's arXiv preprint database and translates it into plain English for general audiences. Every paper gets three things: a plain-language subtitle (8–12 words capturing the core idea), a 2–3 sentence summary leading with what was found, and a "why it matters" explanation focused on real-world consequences.

The site currently has 1201 papers in its archive across 9 subject areas: AI, Computer Science, Physics, Mathematics, Biology, Finance, Statistics, Engineering, Economics. New papers are added automatically twice daily (7 AM and 7 PM UTC). Only first-version arXiv submissions from the past 30 days are considered. Papers are scored for quality signals: venue acceptance (NeurIPS, ICML, Nature, PNAS, etc.), cross-disciplinary listings, and appropriate length.

## How content is structured

Each paper entry contains:
- Formal arXiv title and authors
- Plain-English subtitle — a one-phrase translation of the paper's core idea
- Summary — 2–3 sentences leading with the finding, not the method
- Why it matters — real-world consequences, stated directly
- Link to the full paper on arXiv
- Category and posting date

## Site structure

- Home / archive: https://paperplaine.com (paginated, 12 papers per page)
- Per-category pages: https://paperplaine.com/<category-slug>
- Per-paper pages: https://paperplaine.com/papers/<slug>
- RSS feed: https://paperplaine.com/feed.xml
- llms.txt (this file): https://paperplaine.com/llms.txt
- llms-full.txt (full text of recent papers): https://paperplaine.com/llms-full.txt
- Sitemap: https://paperplaine.com/sitemap.xml

## 10 most recent papers

### Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/democratizing-cross-project-knowledge
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Oriol Alàs, Ian Palacín, Iván Cester et al.
- arXiv: 2611.26398
- Plain-English subtitle: AI that finds buried climate knowledge across European research projects
- Summary: Researchers built an AI system that searches through thousands of scattered research documents from EU water and climate projects, finding relevant information 26.7% more reliably than conventional search methods. The system uses specialized AI models trained on climate and water data, plus a smart controller that decides where to look next based on what it has already found.
- Why it matters: Water managers and climate planners often make decisions without knowing what other projects have already learned — not because the knowledge doesn't exist, but because it's buried in hundreds of unconnected reports. This system lets them ask questions and get targeted answers from across multiple projects at once, reducing duplicated work and helping cities and regions respond faster to water scarcity and climate threats.

### Neckpinches in a Positively Curved Market: Ricci Flow with Surgery on the Nikkei-225
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/neckpinches-in-a-positively
- Category: Physics
- Authors: Siddharta Laloux, Bhargavi Srinivasan
- arXiv: 2611.25860
- Plain-English subtitle: Finding hidden groups of stocks by measuring how curved their relationships are
- Summary: Researchers used a mathematical technique called Ricci flow to map the hidden geometry of relationships between 226 stocks in Japan's Nikkei-225 index. The method automatically discovered 29 natural groups of stocks that almost perfectly align with industry sectors—banks clustered with banks, insurers with insurers, shipping companies together—without being told what industries existed.
- Why it matters: Stock traders and portfolio managers typically group companies by hand-labeled industry categories, but this method finds real clusters from the actual data, which could reveal overlooked relationships between stocks. Because each cluster turned out to be internally more correlated than with the rest of the market, investors could use this to build more effective diversified portfolios or spot when stocks are behaving unexpectedly.

### When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/when-should-deployed-bci
- Category: Quantitative Biology
- Authors: Sergey Musienko
- arXiv: 2611.25315
- Plain-English subtitle: Should brain implants automatically retune themselves, or stay put?
- Summary: Brain-computer interfaces that read brain signals often need to adjust as the user's brain patterns drift over time—but constantly retuning wastes resources and can backfire on clean data. This study shows that adaptation should be selective and capped: a lightweight decision layer picks when to retune and how much, cutting unnecessary adjustments by 87% on stable sessions while matching accuracy of full retraining at 23 times faster speed.
- Why it matters: Brain implants currently either retune blindly (wasting power and time) or never adjust (losing accuracy). A smarter control system that decides *when* to adapt means implanted decoders can run longer on battery, respond faster to real drift, and avoid false corrections when nothing has changed—all without harming accuracy.

### GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/glide-a-fast-calibrated
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Sahibzada Allahyar, Julia White, Dhruv Atreja et al.
- arXiv: 2611.26509
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching AI to make fast, confident choices without explaining its reasoning
- Summary: Researchers created GLiDE, a family of AI models that can score and pick between answers in a single pass—without generating text or step-by-step reasoning. By learning from reasoning models through a technique called distillation, GLiDE kept much of the accuracy boost that comes from reasoning while staying 10 to 100 times faster, with the largest version reaching 73.37% accuracy on a standard benchmark while maintaining reliable confidence calibration.
- Why it matters: Real-time decision-making systems like search results, recommendations, or customer service chatbots currently face a hard trade-off: reason carefully and be slow, or answer fast and risk mistakes. GLiDE collapses that trade-off, making it possible to deploy high-accuracy, confidence-aware decisions in latency-critical settings like mobile apps or live services where waiting 5+ seconds for an answer isn't an option.

### Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/vibe-trading-towards-agent
- Category: Quantitative Finance
- Authors: Haozhe Wu, Zhonghang Li, Chao Huang
- arXiv: 2611.24845
- Plain-English subtitle: Building AI traders that remember why they made each decision
- Summary: Financial markets move too fast for AI agents to work reliably if they lose track of which data fed which decision. Vibe-Trading is a system that keeps trading agents anchored to the specific time, information, and reasoning behind each recommendation—so when prices change, traders know exactly what's become stale and what still holds. It chains together market research, strategy testing, and execution while maintaining an audit trail that lets humans verify and approve trades before they happen.
- Why it matters: AI-powered trading is already happening, but most systems treat each decision as disconnected from its context—risking costly mistakes when conditions shift. Vibe-Trading's traceability and verification layer gives traders and regulators a way to understand why an agent acted, replay its logic, and catch dangerous reasoning before money moves. This matters especially for high-frequency decisions where a stale signal or misaligned authority can wipe out capital in seconds.

### Simple Private Noisy SGD is Minimax-Optimal under Population Strong Convexity
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/simple-private-noisy-sgd
- Category: Statistics
- Authors: Valentin Roth, Marco Avella Medina
- arXiv: 2611.26515
- Plain-English subtitle: When privacy protections don't slow down machine learning as much as we thought
- Summary: Adding noise to protect privacy in machine learning doesn't have to make models less accurate than the best possible performance. Researchers proved that a simple noise-injection technique called Noisy SGD can achieve optimal accuracy rates even when privacy is required, matching what the best non-private algorithms achieve. For logistic regression—a workhorse method in statistics—this eliminates gaps in earlier analyses.
- Why it matters: Machine learning systems increasingly handle sensitive data like medical records and financial information. If privacy safeguards forced companies to accept significantly lower accuracy, the tradeoff might be too steep to use them. This result shows the safeguards don't come with the efficiency penalty researchers feared, making it practical to train accurate models on private data without sacrificing statistical performance.

### AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/agentrobocritic-understanding-the-capability
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Yiyang Du, Yuxuan Kuang, Qitao Zhao et al.
- arXiv: 2611.26613
- Plain-English subtitle: What makes advanced AI robots succeed or fail at manipulation tasks
- Summary: Researchers used a new technique called AgentRoboCritic to analyze how frontier AI agents like GPT-6 Astra control robots at the action level, rather than just measuring whether entire tasks succeed or fail. The analysis revealed these agents can recover from mistakes, understand objects correctly across different scenes, and perform complex manipulation without task-specific training—but still struggle with specific physical challenges like grasping and precise alignment.
- Why it matters: As AI systems take on more physical robot tasks, understanding exactly where and why they fail becomes critical for safe deployment. This framework and dataset enable researchers to spot systematic weaknesses—like consistent failures at grasping—rather than just seeing that "60% of tasks succeeded," making it possible to target improvements where they matter most.

### Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/visual-attribution-limits-and
- Category: Computer Science
- Authors: Haocheng Mei, Yuchuan Tian, Yingte Shu et al.
- arXiv: 2611.26508
- Plain-English subtitle: Can you trust which AI model actually made your video?
- Summary: Researchers tested whether you can verify which video-generation service actually created a file you received, rather than a cheaper substitute. They found that only cryptographic signatures from one provider (BytePlus) reliably proved what was promised, while visual fingerprints fail once videos are re-encoded or compressed—dropping from 84% accuracy to 45% after basic processing.
- Why it matters: Video-generation APIs charge different prices for different models and quality tiers, but intermediaries could pocket the difference by substituting cheaper services without detection. This work shows what auditing can and cannot prove, helping customers and regulators distinguish real fraud from legitimate processing, and revealing that most providers lack the authentication needed to catch deliberate substitution.

### Optimal Control in Pairs Trading with Negative-Power Utility
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/optimal-control-in-pairs
- Category: Mathematics
- Authors: Aleksei Kozhevnikov
- arXiv: 2611.26568
- Plain-English subtitle: How to bet on market mispricings without losing everything
- Summary: Mathematicians solved the problem of how to best invest money in pairs trading—a strategy where you bet that two related stock prices will move back together. Using a new approach to a classic optimization equation, they found explicit formulas for how much to invest and when, and proved these strategies never let your account go negative. The results show that when interest rates are low enough, your wealth stays bounded and predictable; when rates are higher, wealth can spike unpredictably, and there's a point in time beyond which expected returns become infinite even though the optimal strategy itself remains sensible.
- Why it matters: Pairs trading is a real strategy used by hedge funds and algorithmic traders to profit from temporary price misalignments. This paper gives traders the first explicit, proven-optimal playbook for sizing positions and deciding when to buy or sell, without relying on approximations or simulations. The sharp prediction about when expected wealth explodes—even as the strategy stays rational—explains a real practical danger: at certain market conditions and time horizons, the math says your best move is still a risky one.

### TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/tidecache-efficient-hybrid-llm
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Jinbin Luo, Xiaozhe Yao, Shang Yang et al.
- arXiv: 2611.26619
- Plain-English subtitle: Making AI language models faster by smartly sharing memory between chips
- Summary: TideCache is a system that lets AI language models run faster on specialized hardware by automatically managing where to store the data they need—whether that's on the fast GPU chip or slower main memory. The system completes up to twice as many conversation turns per session and cuts response time delays by 20–59%, while speeding up initial response time by up to 3x compared with existing approaches.
- Why it matters: As AI models get bigger and more complex, the bottleneck isn't computing speed—it's managing memory efficiently. TideCache lets companies run these models on existing hardware without buying expensive upgrades, cutting costs while handling more simultaneous users. For applications like customer service agents or coding assistants, faster response times and higher throughput mean better user experience and lower infrastructure spend.
